name: SLAP lesion (superior labral tear)
populations: adults of working and athletic age
older adults (often an incidental imaging finding)
summary: A tear of the superior labrum around the biceps anchor, from throwing peel-back, traction or a fall onto the arm. Labral findings are common without symptoms, so rehabilitation comes first and surgery is contested.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Rehabilitation first: athletes who completed non-operative rehabilitation had about 20 physiotherapy sessions, and return to play was generally within 6 months

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Non-operative care: 78% returned to play if they completed rehabilitation (53.7% overall); return to prior performance 72% in completers (42.6% overall)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: No single test is accurate alone. Biceps Load II had LR+ 1.7 and LR- 0.39 in one study; compression–rotation had the best pooled LR+ (2.81)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI or MR arthrography, read with caution: superior labral tears were reported on MRI in 55% and 72% of asymptomatic 45–60-year-olds (two readers)

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Working and athletic adults: mean age 37.5 years in the original series and 40 years in the sham-controlled trial

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: 6% to 26% of shoulder arthroscopies; US diagnosis rate rose from 28.0 to 142.4 per 100,000 between 2003 and 2013

overview:
A SLAP (superior labrum anterior and posterior) lesion is an injury of the superior glenoid labrum that begins posteriorly, extends anteriorly and includes the anchor of the long head of biceps to the labrum. Snyder and colleagues named it after finding 27 cases among more than 700 shoulder arthroscopies; the commonest mechanism in that series was a compression force from a fall onto an outstretched arm, and the typical complaints were overhead pain and painful catching or popping [r1]. Later series add traction injuries and repetitive overhead throwing, where a torsional peel-back of the posterosuperior labrum is proposed to produce and extend posterior type II lesions [r2,r3].

A labral tear is not the same as a painful shoulder. Radiologists reported superior labral tears on MRI in 55% and 72% of 53 asymptomatic adults aged 45–60 years [r4], and labral pathology in 69% of shoulders in 50 asymptomatic elite climbers [r5]. In arthroscopy series, isolated SLAP lesions are uncommon and most coexist with other intra-articular lesions [r6]. No single clinical test is accurate enough to diagnose the lesion alone [r7,r8], and experienced arthroscopists disagree on the type [r9].

A trial of structured rehabilitation is the usual first step. In a systematic review of athletes, 78% of those who completed non-operative rehabilitation returned to play [r10]. The only sham-controlled trial (118 people with an isolated type II lesion and more than 3 months of pain unresponsive to conventional care) found no significant difference at 2 years between labral repair, biceps tenodesis and sham surgery, and all three groups improved [r11]. Every arm received the same structured rehabilitation, so the trial cannot say whether rehabilitation alone would match these results. Surgery remains an option for selected people, but the evidence does not show that it outperforms placebo plus rehabilitation.

epidemiology.text: In a retrospective review of 530 shoulder arthroscopies by three Belgian surgeons, 32 (6%) showed a SLAP lesion and 53% of those were type II [r3]. In a prospective series of 544 arthroscopies, 139 (26%) showed one: 74% were type I, 21% type II, 0.7% type III and 4% type IV, and 123 of the 139 coexisted with other intra-articular lesions [r6]. The original series had 23 men and 4 women with a mean age of 37.5 years [r1]. The wide range between series reflects the population studied and each surgeon's threshold for calling a lesion. Diagnosis has grown: in US private insurance claims the SLAP diagnosis rate rose from 28.0 to 142.4 per 100,000 between 2003 and 2013, while the proportion of diagnosed patients who had surgery fell; isolated arthroscopic repairs peaked in 2009 at 28.4 per 100,000 and then plateaued, and biceps tenodesis made up 18.1% of SLAP surgeries by 2013 [r12]. Because labral findings on MRI are common in people without symptoms [r4,r5], diagnosis counts overstate symptomatic disease.

intrinsic: Age: type II lesions in people aged 40 years or younger were associated with a Bankart lesion, and those in people over 40 with a supraspinatus tear and humeral head osteoarthritis [r6]
Older age also brings a high background rate of MRI-reported superior labral tears without symptoms (55% and 72% by two readers at 45–60 years) [r4]

Rotation deficit, posterior capsule tightness and scapular dyskinesis in throwers are commonly proposed contributors, but the sources reviewed did not quantify them (see the internal impingement page)
extrinsic: Repetitive overhead throwing: baseball, softball and weightlifting were the commonest sports in the non-operative athlete series [r10]
Mechanism mix in one surgical series: compression 28%, overhead sport 25% and traction 22% [r3]
A fall onto the outstretched arm with the shoulder abducted and slightly flexed was the commonest mechanism in the original series [r1]
Type III and IV lesions were associated with a high-demand occupation and a Bankart lesion [r6]

mechanism.summary: Three mechanisms are described. Compression is a fall onto the outstretched arm with the shoulder abducted and slightly forward flexed, the commonest in the original series [r1]. Traction is a sudden pull on the arm or a forceful biceps contraction that loads the biceps anchor. In throwers, the late-cocking position (about 90° abduction and maximal external rotation) is proposed to produce a torsional peel-back of the posterosuperior labrum by the biceps anchor [r2]. In one series traction accounted for 22% of mechanisms, compression 28% and overhead sport 25% [r3].
sequence: The thrower brings the arm into late cocking: abducted to about 90° and maximally externally rotated.
In this position the biceps anchor transmits torsion to the posterosuperior labrum, which is proposed to peel back off the glenoid rim [r2].
Repeated cycles, or one forceful cycle, detach the labrum and biceps anchor from the superior glenoid; the detachment starts posteriorly and can extend anteriorly [r1].
In acceleration and deceleration the biceps and posterior cuff resist the moving arm, so traction loads the already weakened anchor (a proposed contributor, not measured in these sources).
A posterior component allows posterosuperior instability, with a secondary anteroinferior pseudolaxity (the drive-through sign at arthroscopy) [r13].
Chronic superior instability may be followed by partial articular-sided rotator cuff tears; cuff tears were present in 31% of 102 type II lesions [r13].
The detached margin catches or pops in overhead positions, giving deep pain with mechanical symptoms [r1].

variants.name: Compression (fall onto the arm)
variants.description: A fall onto the outstretched arm with the shoulder abducted and slightly forward flexed. The commonest mechanism in the original series [r1] and 28% in a Belgian series [r3].

variants.name: Traction
variants.description: A sudden pull on the arm or a forceful biceps contraction, for example catching a heavy object or deceleration of a throw. Traction accounted for 22% of mechanisms in one series [r3].

variants.name: Repetitive overhead throwing (peel-back)
variants.description: Gradual onset in throwers, with a torsional peel-back of the posterosuperior labrum in late cocking proposed as the mechanism [r2]. Overhead sport accounted for 25% of mechanisms in one series [r3].

variants.name: Age-related or incidental
variants.description: Superior labral tears are read on MRI in more than half of asymptomatic people aged 45–60 years, and the authors suggest many may be normal age-related findings [r4]. Symptoms and examination, not the scan, decide whether a tear matters.

variants.name: Combined lesions
variants.description: SLAP lesions often coexist with a Bankart lesion in people aged 40 years or younger, and with cuff tears and humeral head osteoarthritis in older people [r6]. Symptoms should not be ascribed to the labrum when other lesions are present [r6].

anatomy.text: The superior labrum is the fibrocartilaginous rim at the top of the glenoid. It deepens the socket and is the main attachment of the long head of biceps tendon, which arises from the supraglenoid tubercle and blends with the superior labrum. Capsular ligaments attach to the labrum around the glenoid rim. Normal variants of the anterosuperior labrum (for example an extra-large sublabral hole) can be mistaken for tears, and Handelberg and colleagues warned of diagnostic and therapeutic errors from them [r3]. Dynamic stability comes from the rotator cuff, which compresses the head into the socket, and the scapular muscles that position the glenoid. The biceps-labral complex stabilises the head against superior and posterosuperior translation in the cocked throwing position.

structures.name: Superior glenoid labrum
structures.role: Fibrocartilage rim that deepens the socket and anchors the biceps tendon and capsule; the site of the SLAP lesion

structures.name: Long head of biceps tendon and its anchor
structures.role: Arises from the supraglenoid tubercle and superior labrum; transmits traction and torsion to the labrum, especially in late cocking and deceleration

structures.name: Posterosuperior labrum and capsule
structures.role: Region peeled off the glenoid rim in the proposed peel-back mechanism [r2]

structures.name: Supraspinatus and infraspinatus (articular side)
structures.role: Dynamic stabilisers whose articular-sided fibres can develop partial tears secondary to superior instability [r13]

structures.name: Glenohumeral capsule and ligaments
structures.role: Static restraints that attach to the labrum; the anteroinferior labrum (Bankart region) is a separate site that often coexists [r6]

structures.name: Scapular stabilisers (serratus anterior, lower trapezius)
structures.role: Position the glenoid under the humeral head; scapular stabilisation is a core part of non-operative programs [r14]

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
In Snyder's description the injury begins posteriorly, extends anteriorly and stops before or at the mid-glenoid notch, including the biceps anchor [r1]. The pattern ranges from simple fraying of the free labral edge (type I, 74% of 139 SLAP lesions) to detachment of the labrum and biceps anchor from the glenoid (type II, 21%), bucket-handle tears (types III and IV) and combinations with a Bankart lesion [r6]. Only types II, IV and V are considered unstable and in need of fixation [r3]. Type II lesions with a posterior component produce posterosuperior instability, shown at arthroscopy as a drive-through sign that disappears after repair of the posterior component [r13].

Structure and symptoms correlate poorly. The labrum is fibrocartilage with a limited blood supply, so whether a detached margin re-attaches is uncertain, and none of the sources reviewed measured labral healing. Most SLAP lesions coexist with other intra-articular lesions, and care is needed when ascribing symptoms to the labrum [r6]. A sham-controlled trial found that surgical fixation of an isolated type II lesion gave no benefit over diagnostic arthroscopy plus rehabilitation [r11].

structures.name: Superior labrum and biceps anchor
structures.effect: Fraying (type I), detachment from the glenoid rim (type II), bucket-handle tear (type III) or bucket-handle tear extending into the biceps tendon (type IV) [r6,r1]

structures.name: Posterosuperior labrum
structures.effect: Torsional peel-back in the cocked position is proposed to produce and extend posterior type II lesions [r2]

structures.name: Rotator cuff (articular side)
structures.effect: Partial articular-sided tears occurred in 31% of 102 type II lesions, specific to lesion location, and are attributed to chronic superior instability [r13]

structures.name: Anteroinferior labrum (Bankart lesion)
structures.effect: Associated with type II lesions in people aged 40 years or younger; this changes the diagnosis and the surgical plan [r6]

structures.name: Humeral head cartilage
structures.effect: Osteoarthritis of the humeral head was associated with type II lesions in people over 40 years [r6]

muscles.name: Long head of biceps
muscles.effect: Pain on resisted flexion and supination and tenderness over the bicipital groove; it is the force that tractions the anchor, so heavy or fast biceps loading often provokes symptoms

muscles.name: Supraspinatus and infraspinatus
muscles.effect: Pain inhibition and weakness in provocative positions; partial articular-sided cuff tears can develop with superior instability [r13]

muscles.name: Scapular stabilisers (serratus anterior, lower and middle trapezius)
muscles.effect: Delayed or reduced activation and dyskinesis are common; non-operative programs emphasise scapular stabilisation [r14]

muscles.name: Posterior cuff and capsule
muscles.effect: Tightness and loss of internal rotation are common in throwers, and posterior capsular stretching was part of a reported non-operative program [r14]

cellular.description: After an acute injury, local bleeding then neutrophils and macrophages clear debris. Many SLAP lesions are not acute, and type I fraying is often degenerative, so this phase may be absent.
Fibroblasts lay down disorganised collagen and new capillaries form where there is a blood supply. The fibrocartilaginous labrum is poorly vascularised, so the detached edge may not re-attach firmly.
Collagen aligns along lines of load. Whether a detached labrum reliably re-attaches was not measured in the sources reviewed, which is why muscle control carries much of the stability.

systems.effect: Pain does not track structure: labral tears are common without symptoms [r4,r5], and a sham-surgery group improved as much as the surgical groups [r11], so pain processing and load tolerance matter as much as the labral lesion.
Expectation effects are strong: 19 of 26 patients (73%) in the sham group believed they had been repaired [r11]. Fear of the 'torn labrum' label can drive avoidance.
In throwers, trunk and hip drive, thoracic rotation, scapular control and glenohumeral rotation range all change the load on the biceps-labral complex (see the internal impingement page).
Synovitis and capsular irritation accompany a symptomatic episode and settle with relative rest and load management.

Diagnosis rose from 28.0 to 142.4 per 100,000 between 2003 and 2013 while the share of those diagnosed having surgery fell [r12], consistent with growing awareness and imaging, and a risk of treating scans.

grading.system: Snyder classification (types I–IV), with the Morgan subtypes of type II and later combined patterns (Maffet and others)

grades.description: Fraying and degeneration of the free edge of the superior labrum; the labral attachment and biceps anchor are intact.
grades.prognosis: The commonest arthroscopic finding (74% of 139 SLAP lesions) [r6]. Not considered unstable or in need of fixation [r3]; often degenerative.

grades.description: The superior labrum and biceps anchor are detached from the glenoid, so the anchor is unstable. Morgan's subtypes by location: anterior, posterior or combined.
grades.prognosis: 21% of 139 SLAP lesions [r6]. Of 102 type II lesions, 37% were anterior, 31% posterior and 31% combined [r13]. The type studied in repair and tenodesis trials, including the sham-controlled trial [r11].

grades.description: Bucket-handle tear of the superior labrum with an intact biceps anchor.
grades.prognosis: Rare (one of 139) [r6]. Surgeons treat type III lesions more variably than any other type [r9].

grades.description: Bucket-handle tear of the superior labrum that extends into the biceps tendon.
grades.prognosis: 4% of SLAP lesions [r6]. Considered unstable [r3]. Surgeons found types III and IV hard to tell apart [r9].

grades.grade: Type V and later combined patterns
grades.description: A Bankart lesion that continues superiorly with biceps anchor detachment (type V) and other combined patterns added by Maffet and others.
grades.prognosis: Type V is considered unstable [r3]. Management is driven by the associated Bankart or capsular lesion.

timeframes.summary: Natural history is poorly described. In athletes, non-operative treatment generally allowed return to play within 6 months [r10]. After repair or tenodesis the process is longer: in the sham-controlled trial a sling was used for 3 weeks, biceps loading began at 12 weeks, and rehabilitation continued for 3–6 months with 12–16 therapist sessions [r11].

healing.phase: Irritable phase: settle and modify load
healing.description: Reduce provocative overhead and heavy biceps loading, keep the shoulder moving in comfortable range, start scapular and cuff activation.
Restore range, address posterior capsule tightness if present, and build scapular and rotator cuff endurance.
Progressive strengthening including the kinetic chain, with graded biceps loading and overhead exposure.
Plyometrics and an interval throwing or sport-specific program, criteria-based.

healing.phase: Protected phase after repair or tenodesis (if surgery)
healing.description: A sling for about 3 weeks in the trial [r11]; external rotation beyond 0° was avoided for 3 weeks after a posterosuperior repair in one described protocol [r2]. Follow the surgeon's protocol.

milestones.label: Resting pain settled and sleeping comfortably
Full pain-free movement, posterior tightness addressed
Graded biceps loading under way
milestones.note: Began at 12 weeks after surgery in the sham-controlled trial [r11]

milestones.label: Interval throwing or sport-specific program starts
Return to play after non-operative care
milestones.note: Generally under 6 months in the studies that reported timing [r10]

timeframes.returnToSport: Criteria-based. In athletes managed non-operatively, return to play generally occurred within 6 months [r10]. After surgery, return commonly takes 6 months or longer (clinical convention), and return rates in throwers vary widely: 37.5% to 94.7% after SLAP repair and 35.3% to 93.1% after biceps tenodesis in a systematic review of 16 studies, with baseball pitchers doing worst [r15].

symptoms: Deep, poorly localised shoulder pain with overhead activity, often worse in late cocking and acceleration in throwers [r1]
Painful catching, clicking or popping in the shoulder [r1]
Pain with heavy pulling or lifting, or with the biceps loaded in a stretched position
Loss of throwing velocity or control, and a feeling of the arm not 'coming through'
Symptoms are often vague and inconsistent, and do not identify a SLAP lesion reliably [r3]
signs: Usually a normal-looking shoulder without swelling or deformity
Pain or a click deep in the shoulder on labral provocation tests, which are individually unreliable [r7,r8]
Tenderness at the bicipital groove or anterior shoulder
Loss of internal rotation or total rotation arc in throwers, and scapular dyskinesis
Rotator cuff pain on resisted testing, and sometimes weakness if a cuff tear coexists [r13]

subjective: Mechanism: fall onto the outstretched arm (compression), a pull or catch (traction), or repetitive throwing, and the specific phase of the movement that hurts
Onset, duration and trajectory: a longer symptomatic period was associated with failure of non-operative care [r10]
Sport, position, throwing volume, recent changes in load, and level of competition
Mechanical symptoms (catching, clicking, locking), night pain, and function in daily tasks
Previous dislocation or instability (Bankart lesion) and previous shoulder surgery
Beliefs about the diagnosis and the MRI result, expectations about surgery, and goals
observation: Muscle bulk of supraspinatus, infraspinatus and deltoid (cuff tear or suprascapular nerve involvement)
Resting scapular position and dyskinesis during elevation and lowering
Posture: forward head, thoracic kyphosis and shoulder protraction in throwers and weightlifters
palpation: Bicipital groove and long head of biceps tenderness
Anterior and posterior joint line, and the greater tuberosity for cuff involvement
AC joint, to separate AC pain, which pain 'on top' with the O'Brien test suggests
rangeOfMotion: Glenohumeral internal and external rotation at 90° abduction in supine, comparing total arc with the other side
Elevation and horizontal adduction: posterior capsule and cuff tightness
Cervical and thoracic spine screen for referred or contributory pain
strength: Resisted external and internal rotation, and abduction and scaption, with a hand-held dynamometer if available
Resisted elbow flexion and forearm supination: biceps pain
Scapular strength and endurance (serratus anterior, lower trapezius)
External rotation lag or drop-arm signs if a cuff tear is suspected, particularly over 40 years [r6]
neuro: Cervical screen: Spurling, upper limb tension and dermatomal, myotomal and reflex testing to exclude cervical radiculopathy
Suprascapular nerve: infraspinatus bulk and external rotation strength, if a paralabral cyst is suspected
Neurovascular screen of the hand if the history is traumatic
functional: Overhead reach, hand behind head and hand behind back
Closed-chain upper limb stability, such as a wall push-up plus and quadruped weight shifts
Sport-specific tasks: throwing mechanics, overhead press, bench press and pulling movements
Kinetic-chain screen: single-leg balance and squat, trunk rotation and hip internal rotation

specialTests.name: O'Brien (active compression) test
specialTests.purpose: Labral tear and biceps anchor involvement; separates deep labral pain from AC joint pain
specialTests.procedure: Standing, arm flexed to 90° with the elbow extended and adducted about 10–15° across the body, thumb down. The examiner pushes down while the patient resists, then repeats with the palm up.
specialTests.positive: Pain or a painful click deep inside the shoulder with the thumb down that is reduced or abolished with the palm up. Pain on top of the shoulder points to the AC joint. The original excellent figures were not replicated by later research, and no test, including this one, showed diagnostic utility for any SLAP lesion in a strict-design study [r7,r8].

specialTests.name: Speed's test
specialTests.purpose: Biceps tendon and superior labrum provocation
specialTests.procedure: Resist shoulder flexion at about 90° with the elbow extended and the forearm supinated.
specialTests.positive: Pain at the bicipital groove or deep in the shoulder. In pooled data the test had low sensitivity and modest specificity for SLAP lesions, so it neither rules in nor rules out a tear [r16].

specialTests.name: Yergason's test
specialTests.procedure: Elbow flexed to 90° and tucked at the side; the patient resists forearm supination (and external rotation) against the examiner.
specialTests.positive: Pain at the bicipital groove or deep in the shoulder. Among tests meta-analysed for SLAP lesions this one had the best specificity, while no pooled test had sensitivity above 52%, and the review could not recommend any single test for a firm diagnosis [r7].

specialTests.name: Biceps Load II test
specialTests.procedure: Supine, arm abducted to about 120° and externally rotated to apprehension with the forearm supinated. The patient flexes the elbow against resistance while the examiner watches for a change in pain.
specialTests.positive: Pain that persists or increases with the resisted elbow flexion. Initially reported with excellent accuracy, but it failed to replicate [r7]. In a strict-design study of 87 patients it was the only test with any utility for an isolated SLAP lesion, with a PPV of 26% and NPV of 93%, and none worked for any SLAP lesion including those with other disorders [r8].

specialTests.name: Compression–rotation test
specialTests.purpose: Labral tear with a mechanical component
specialTests.procedure: Supine or lateral decubitus with the arm abducted to about 90° and the elbow flexed; the examiner applies axial compression through the humerus while circumducting and rotating the arm.
specialTests.positive: A painful catch, click or reproduction of symptoms. It had the best pooled LR+ among SLAP tests, but it is still modest [r7]. A positive result also predicted failure of non-operative treatment in one cohort [r10].

specialTests.name: Crank test
specialTests.procedure: Arm elevated to about 160° in the scapular plane with the elbow flexed; the examiner applies axial load while rotating the humerus internally and externally.
specialTests.positive: Pain with or without a click. No accuracy figures are quoted because none were found in the sources reviewed; it was one of the baseline tests recorded in the sham-controlled trial [r11].

clinicalRules.name: No single test or cluster is enough
clinicalRules.description: In 87 patients with confirmation by arthroscopy, no test cluster had better diagnostic accuracy than stand-alone tests, and no test worked for SLAP lesions with coexisting disorders [r8]. Individual tests have limited accuracy and combinations add only marginally [r7]. Use the history, the whole examination and response to treatment, not one provocation test.

clinicalRules.name: Location hints in surgical series (not a validated rule)
clinicalRules.description: In a surgical series of 102 type II lesions, Speed's and O'Brien's tests were useful for predicting anterior lesions, and the Jobe relocation test for posterior lesions [r13]. Treat this as hypothesis-generating.

clinicalRules.name: Look for the company the lesion keeps
clinicalRules.description: Most SLAP lesions coexist with Bankart lesions, cuff tears or osteoarthritis, and isolated lesions are uncommon [r6]. Test the cuff, the anteroinferior and posterior restraints and the cervical spine before settling on the labrum.

outcomeMeasures.name: Western Ontario Shoulder Instability Index (WOSI) and Rowe score
outcomeMeasures.use: Primary outcomes in the sham-controlled trial [r11]

outcomeMeasures.name: American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons (ASES) score and SANE
outcomeMeasures.use: Function and patient-rated shoulder status; ASES was used in a repair cohort and a non-operative case series, and SANE in the repair cohort [r17,r14]

outcomeMeasures.name: Oxford Instability Shoulder Score and EQ-5D
outcomeMeasures.use: Secondary outcomes in the sham-controlled trial [r11]

outcomeMeasures.name: Kerlan-Jobe Orthopaedic Clinic (KJOC) shoulder and elbow score
outcomeMeasures.use: Overhead-athlete function and readiness to throw

outcomeMeasures.name: Hand-held dynamometry and glenohumeral rotation range
outcomeMeasures.use: External and internal rotation strength limb symmetry, and total rotation arc

imaging.indication: Persistent pain, older athletes or suspected bony pathology
imaging.findings: Excludes glenohumeral or AC joint osteoarthritis and fracture. A Bennett spur was among factors linked with failure of non-operative care [r10].

imaging.indication: Persistent symptoms despite a trial of rehabilitation, suspected cuff tear or paralabral cyst, or surgical planning; not to confirm the diagnosis in isolation
imaging.findings: Superior labral signal change or detachment, paralabral cyst and partial cuff tear. In 132 patients with positive examination signs awaiting surgery, MRI sensitivity was 70.59% and specificity 40%, and its classification matched arthroscopy in 52 (39%) [r18]. Two radiologists read superior labral tears in 55% and 72% of asymptomatic 45–60-year-olds, with only moderate agreement (kappa 0.410) [r4]. MRI arthrography selected patients for the sham-controlled trial, but its authors note that the validity of clinical tests, arthroscopy and MRI arthrography is questioned [r11].

imaging.indication: Reserved for people who fail adequate rehabilitation and are considering surgery
imaging.findings: Not infallible: experienced surgeons struggled to distinguish normal shoulders from type II tears and types III from IV, with only moderate repeat agreement [r9]. In a sham-controlled trial, 65 of 183 patients who had arthroscopy were excluded at surgery because they did not have an isolated type II lesion [r11].

imaging.indication: Suspected rotator cuff tear, particularly over 40 years
imaging.findings: Partial or full-thickness cuff tear; limited value for the labrum itself

differentials.name: Internal impingement in the overhead athlete
differentials.distinguishing: Posterior shoulder pain in late cocking in throwers, often with a rotation deficit; frequently coexists with a posterosuperior labral lesion.

differentials.name: Rotator cuff related shoulder pain
differentials.distinguishing: Painful arc and pain with resisted abduction or rotation, without mechanical catching; common coexisting source of pain.

differentials.name: Long head of biceps tendinopathy
differentials.distinguishing: Anterior pain over the bicipital groove with resisted flexion and supination; may coexist with a SLAP lesion.

differentials.name: Anterior shoulder instability (Bankart lesion)
differentials.distinguishing: Dislocation or subluxation history, apprehension and positive relocation tests; the Bankart lesion often coexists with a type II SLAP lesion in people aged 40 years or younger [r6].

differentials.name: Posterior shoulder instability
differentials.distinguishing: Pain and instability with a flexed, adducted and internally rotated arm, and a positive jerk or Kim test.

differentials.name: Multidirectional instability
differentials.distinguishing: Generalised laxity, a positive sulcus sign and symptoms in several directions; labral tears can coexist.

differentials.name: Traumatic rotator cuff tear
differentials.distinguishing: Sudden weakness and difficulty elevating after a fall, particularly over 40 years; cuff tears occurred with 31% of type II lesions in one series [r13].

differentials.name: Acromioclavicular joint injury or osteolysis
differentials.distinguishing: Pain localised on top of the shoulder, tender AC joint and pain with horizontal adduction.

differentials.name: Cervical radiculopathy
differentials.distinguishing: Neck-origin pain, dermatomal symptoms and reproduction with Spurling or neck movements.

redFlags: Constant night or rest pain not related to movement, unexplained weight loss, fever or a history of cancer: possible infection or malignancy. Refer urgently for medical review and imaging.

Neurological deficit (myotomal weakness, dermatomal numbness or reflex change): cervical radiculopathy or brachial plexus problem. If it is isolated infraspinatus wasting and weakness, consider suprascapular nerve compression, for example by a paralabral cyst, and refer for imaging and nerve assessment.
Acute traumatic dislocation or a pale, cold or pulseless hand after injury: emergency department. Document the axillary nerve and distal pulses.
Sudden loss of elevation or weakness after a fall, particularly over 40 years: possible rotator cuff tear [r6]. Arrange imaging and orthopaedic review.
Shoulder pain with chest pressure, breathlessness or sweating, or pain unrelated to shoulder movement: consider cardiac or visceral referral and seek urgent medical assessment.

After surgery: fever, wound drainage, spreading erythema or severe escalating pain suggest infection; refer back to the surgeon the same day. Painful stiffness (capsulitis) occurred in 10 of 118 trial patients (5 after repair, 4 after tenodesis, 1 after sham surgery) [r11].

No meaningful improvement after about 3 months of well-delivered, adherent rehabilitation: reassess the diagnosis, look for coexisting lesions and refer for a surgical opinion rather than repeating the same program.

management.principles: Start with a clear explanation that labral findings are common in people without pain, so the aim is to restore load tolerance and function, not to fix a scan. Offer a structured rehabilitation program first: nonsurgical management is described as first-line for most SLAP tears in athletes, and those who completed rehabilitation did much better than those who stopped early [r10]. Surgery is an option after an adequate trial, in selected people. The only sham-controlled trial found no benefit of repair or tenodesis over sham surgery in an isolated type II lesion [r11]; observational repair cohorts report improvement but cannot separate it from placebo, rehabilitation and natural history [r17]; older age predicts failure [r17,r10]. Decide together, explain the long recovery and complications of surgery, and match the plan to age, sport, position and goals.

medical.name: Analgesia, NSAIDs and activity modification
medical.description: Short-term analgesia and temporary reduction of provocative overhead and heavy biceps loading to settle the irritable phase. NSAIDs were part of the non-operative package in one case series, but their separate effect is unknown [r14].

medical.name: Arthroscopic SLAP repair (type II)
medical.description: In a double-blind, sham-controlled trial of 118 people (mean age 40) with an isolated type II lesion, labral repair was not better than sham surgery: the 2-year difference in Rowe score was 0.6 points (95% CI −5.9 to 7.0), WOSI findings were similar, and prolonged stiffness occurred in 5 people after repair versus 1 after sham [r11]. In the sham group, 14 of 39 people had surgery between 6 and 24 months (12 repairs), which the authors could not separate from unblinding [r11]. In a prospective cohort of 179 repairs in a young, active population, ASES improved from 65 to 88 but 66 (36.8%) met failure criteria and 50 had revision; the relative risk of failure was 3.45 (95% CI 2.0–4.9) in people older than 36 years [r17]. In overhead throwers, return to play after repair ranged from 37.5% to 94.7%, and 40% to 80% in pitchers [r15]. Reserve for selected people after an adequate trial of rehabilitation, and explain the sham-trial result.

medical.name: Biceps tenodesis (or tenotomy) as the surgical alternative
medical.description: A meta-analysis of 5 comparative cohort studies (234 patients) found higher satisfaction (95.6% versus 76.2%, p = .01) and return to sport (81.3% versus 64.3%, p = .02) after tenodesis than after repair, with similar function and a non-significant trend to fewer reoperations (6.5% versus 14.2%) [r19]. In overhead athletes (13 studies), ASES, return to sport, return to preinjury level and complications did not differ significantly, and the authors called for randomised trials [r20]. In the sham-controlled trial tenodesis was no better than sham surgery [r11]. The evidence is mostly low-level and conflicts with the randomised result.

medical.name: Routine repair in people older than about 36 years
medical.description: In a repair cohort, advanced age was the only factor associated with failure (age over 36 years: relative risk 3.45, 95% CI 2.0–4.9) [r17], and older age was among factors linked with failure of non-operative care too [r10]. The sham-controlled trial found no benefit in a population with a mean age of 40 [r11]. Avoid routine repair; if surgery is chosen, tenodesis is the alternative to discuss.

medical.name: Surgery based on an MRI labral finding alone
medical.description: Superior labral tears are read on MRI in more than half of asymptomatic adults aged 45–60 years [r4] and in a large share of asymptomatic athletes [r5], and surgeons disagree on the type at arthroscopy [r9]. Imaging alone is not an indication for surgery.

physio.name: Structured rehabilitation program as first-line care
physio.description: In a systematic review of five studies of 244 athletes, return to play was 53.7% overall and 78% in those who completed the program; return to prior performance was 42.6% overall and 72% in completers. Athletes who stopped for surgery had a mean of 8 therapy sessions versus 20 in those who succeeded, and pain and ASES scores all improved with non-operative care [r10]. A case series program of NSAIDs, scapular stabilisation and posterior capsular stretching helped those who responded (ASES total 58.5 to 84.7), but 51% of the 39 respondents with a documented lesion went on to surgery and the questionnaire response rate was 16.4% [r14]. The evidence is low-level, mostly case series, but the review concludes that non-operative treatment should be first line for most SLAP tears.

physio.name: Posterior capsule stretching and rotation range work
physio.description: Included in the reported non-operative program [r14]; its separate effect has not been tested. Use where total rotation arc or internal rotation is reduced, and avoid forcing end-range stretches that provoke pain.

physio.name: Scapular, rotator cuff and kinetic-chain strengthening
physio.description: Progressive scapular stabilisation, cuff strengthening and trunk-hip work, then graded biceps loading and overhead exposure, as in the described programs. The trial's rehabilitation, used in all arms, began scapula-humeral rhythm work, then biceps loading at 12 weeks, with 12–16 therapist sessions and 20 self-administered exercises over 3–6 months [r11].

physio.name: Education about imaging findings, prognosis and expectations
physio.description: Explain that labral findings are common without symptoms [r4,r5], that all arms of the sham-controlled trial improved [r11], and that adherence matters [r10]. Agree on load, a graded return to overhead activity and when to revisit surgery.

physio.name: Protected rehabilitation after repair or tenodesis
physio.description: Follow the surgeon's protocol. Described features include a sling for about 3 weeks, avoiding external rotation beyond 0° for 3 weeks after a posterosuperior repair [r2], and graded biceps loading from about 12 weeks [r11].

education: A torn or frayed labrum on a scan does not always explain pain: many people with no pain have the same finding, so we treat the shoulder you have, not the picture.
A structured rehabilitation program is the usual first step, and people who finished it did much better than those who stopped early [r10]. Expect about 3–6 months of work.
In the best trial so far, people who had repair, tenodesis or a sham operation improved by similar amounts, so surgery is a choice to make together after rehabilitation, not an urgent need [r11].
Throwers: your shoulder, shoulder blade, trunk and legs work as one chain. Part of the program builds this chain and a gradual return to throwing.
See your clinician promptly for night pain that does not ease, new weakness or numbness in the arm, fever or a hot, swollen shoulder.

rehab.overview: Progression is criteria-based and the same logic applies to non-operative care and, after the surgeon's protection period, to post-operative care. In the sham-controlled trial, rehabilitation for all groups involved 12–16 therapist sessions and 20 self-administered exercises over 3–6 months, with a sling for 3 weeks, scapula-humeral rhythm and mobility work early, biceps loading from 12 weeks and sport-specific rehabilitation from about 3 months [r11]. Athletes who completed non-operative rehabilitation had about 20 sessions [r10]. Stages and dosages below are typical clinical conventions, and criteria override time. Avoid combined extreme abduction and external rotation and heavy biceps loading early, and progress overhead and throwing exposure only when the shoulder is calm for 24 hours.

stages.name: Settle and keep moving
goals: Maintain comfortable range of motion and sleep
Educate on the diagnosis and the plan
precautions: Avoid end-range cocking (abduction plus external rotation), forced overhead positions and heavy or fast biceps loading
After repair or tenodesis, follow the surgeon's sling and range protocol (for example avoiding external rotation beyond 0° for 3 weeks after a posterosuperior repair [r2])

exercises.name: Pendulum (Codman) swings
exercises.cues: Let the arm hang loose and swing by moving the trunk

exercises.name: Scapular setting (retraction and gentle depression)
exercises.cues: Draw the shoulder blades back and down without shrugging

exercises.name: Submaximal isometric external and internal rotation at the side
exercises.dosage: 5 × 10 s at about 20–30% effort, twice daily (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Elbow bent, arm at the side, press gently into the wall

exercises.name: Supported elevation in the scapular plane to about 90°
exercises.cues: Use the other hand to assist; stay pain-free

progressionCriteria: Resting pain 3/10 or less and sleeping without regular waking
Pain-free elevation to about 120° and comfortable activities of daily living
No mechanical catching in the working range

stages.name: Mobility and scapular-cuff control
goals: Restore full pain-free range and a symmetrical rotation arc
Address posterior capsule and pectoralis minor tightness if present
Build scapular and cuff endurance and control
precautions: Keep stretches below pain; the sleeper stretch can provoke the anterosuperior shoulder, so reduce the range if it does
Avoid heavy biceps loading in a stretched or externally rotated position

exercises.name: Sleeper stretch or cross-body adduction stretch
exercises.cues: Gentle internal rotation or horizontal adduction; stop at first firm stretch, not pain

exercises.name: Side-lying external rotation
exercises.dosage: 2–3 × 15 with a light dumbbell, 3–4 times per week
exercises.cues: Elbow tucked to the ribs, rotate slowly

exercises.name: Band row
exercises.cues: Squeeze the shoulder blades back and down

exercises.name: Scaption raise to 90°
exercises.dosage: 3 × 10–12 with a light dumbbell, 3 times per week
exercises.cues: Thumb up, lift in the scapular plane

exercises.name: Wall slide
exercises.cues: Keep the shoulder blades moving; avoid the head dropping forward

progressionCriteria: Total rotation arc symmetrical or within about 5° of the other side (clinical convention)
Normal scapulohumeral rhythm on elevation and lowering

stages.name: Strength and biceps-labral loading
goals: Restore rotator cuff, scapular and trunk strength
Expose the shoulder to overhead and abducted external rotation positions
precautions: Introduce 90° abduction and external rotation loading gradually, and only when range and scapular control are adequate
Biceps loading started at about 12 weeks after surgery in the trial; use that as a guide only if surgery was performed [r11]

exercises.name: Push-up plus progression (wall, incline, floor)
exercises.cues: Straight trunk, protract fully at the top

exercises.name: Prone Y raise
exercises.cues: Thumbs up, lift with the lower trapezius

exercises.name: External rotation at 90° abduction with a band
exercises.dosage: 3 × 10–12, increasing range gradually, 2–3 times per week
exercises.cues: Stable shoulder blade; stop before the range provokes deep pain

exercises.name: Overhead press (dumbbell)
exercises.cues: Press in the scapular plane, control the lowering

exercises.name: Side plank and bird-dog for trunk and kinetic-chain control
exercises.dosage: 3 × 30–45 s each side, 3 times per week
exercises.cues: Ribs down, hips level, shoulder blade set

progressionCriteria: External and internal rotation strength 90% or more of the other side
Pain-free overhead loading and no mechanical symptoms
Good scapular control during push-up plus and overhead press

stages.name: Power, throwing and return to sport
goals: Develop upper-limb power and plyometric tolerance
Progress through an interval throwing or sport-specific program
Return to full training and competition
precautions: Increase one variable at a time (distance, volume or intensity), with a rest day between throwing sessions
Pitchers and throwers had lower return rates after surgery; plan for a longer return [r15]

exercises.name: Medicine-ball chest pass and overhead throw
Plyometric push-up or ball drops (reactive stability)
exercises.cues: Land with elbows slightly bent and shoulder blades set

exercises.name: Interval throwing program (progressive distance, then volume, then intensity)
exercises.dosage: 3–4 sessions per week, graded over 6–12 weeks (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Quality first; stop if deep pain or mechanical symptoms return

exercises.name: Sport-specific drills (serving, bowling, spiking, pitching with the full kinetic chain)
exercises.dosage: Start at about 25–30% of normal volume and build over 4–6 weeks (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Include the legs and trunk in the pattern

progressionCriteria: Completes the interval throwing or sport program without pain or mechanical symptoms
Strength and function tests meet return-to-sport criteria
Confident and psychologically ready to return

criteria: Full pain-free range of motion with a total rotation arc symmetrical or within about 5° of the other side (clinical convention)
External and internal rotation strength and scapular strength about 90% or more of the other side
No pain or mechanical symptoms on provocative positions and during the full interval throwing or sport-specific program
Good scapular control and kinetic-chain function (trunk rotation, single-leg control, hip rotation)
Agreed graded return of volume and intensity, with symptoms monitored over the next 24 hours
Psychologically ready and confident in the shoulder
Time: commonly within 6 months after non-operative care [r10], and often longer after surgery (clinical convention)
tests: Hand-held dynamometry for external rotation, internal rotation and scaption, compared with the other side
Total rotation arc measured with an inclinometer in supine at 90° abduction
Closed Kinetic Chain Upper Extremity Stability Test
Seated single-arm shot-put or medicine-ball throw
KJOC score and WOSI at the end of rehabilitation

prognosis: With non-operative treatment, athletes who completed the program had a 78% return-to-play rate versus 53.7% for all athletes, and return to prior performance was 72% in completers versus 42.6% overall; factors linked with failure included older age, overhead sports (especially baseball pitchers), traumatic injury, a positive compression–rotation test, concomitant rotator cuff injury, longer symptom duration and a Bennett spur [r10]. In a case series of 39 people with a documented lesion, 51% went on to surgery, while successful non-operative care returned all of those athletes to sport and 66% of overhead athletes to the same level [r14]. In the sham-controlled trial, all three arms improved, with no significant difference at 2 years (Rowe score about 85–87 in all arms); 14 of 39 sham patients had a later operation between 6 and 24 months, and 8 of those 14 had a Rowe score over 80 after reoperation [r11]. After repair in a young, active cohort, 36.8% met failure criteria and 50 of 179 had revision, with failure more likely over 36 years of age [r17]. Return to play after surgery in throwers ranged from 37.5% to 94.7% after repair [r15]. Long-term outcomes of non-operative care beyond 2–3 years were not quantified in the sources reviewed.
prevention: No SLAP-specific prevention trial was identified in the sources reviewed; the following are clinical conventions
Manage throwing volume and rest, with graded increases after a break rather than sudden spikes in pitch count or intensity
Maintain glenohumeral total rotation range, scapular control and rotator cuff strength, and include trunk and hip strength in throwers
Address early deep or mechanical overhead pain before it becomes entrenched; completing a rehabilitation program matters [r10]
Technique review for throwers and weightlifters (for example bench-press depth and grip width)
clinicalPearls: Do not diagnose from one test or from the MRI: tests are individually weak and clustering did not help [r8], and superior labral tears are read on MRI in a large share of pain-free people [r4,r5].

The sham-controlled trial is the key result to quote: repair, tenodesis and sham surgery improved similarly, and 73% of the sham patients who were asked believed they had been repaired [r11]. Expectation, rehabilitation and natural history are powerful.
Adherence predicts success: athletes who stopped rehabilitation for surgery attended about 8 sessions versus 20 in those who succeeded [r10]. Dose the program properly before judging failure.
In a thrower with posterior shoulder pain in late cocking, think internal impingement, rotation deficit and cuff before calling it a SLAP lesion; they often coexist (see internal impingement).
Check for company: Bankart lesions in younger people and cuff tears and osteoarthritis in older people coexist with type II lesions [r6], and the posterior component can drive the cuff changes [r13].

A positive compression–rotation test, traumatic onset, overhead sport and a longer symptom period flag people less likely to respond to non-operative care [r10]; discuss early what happens if progress stalls.

animation.title: How a SLAP lesion happens in a thrower

captions.text: A thrower prepares to throw with the right arm.
In late cocking the arm is abducted and fully externally rotated.
The biceps anchor twists the posterosuperior labrum, the proposed peel-back.
In acceleration and follow-through the biceps pulls on the same attachment.
Repeated cycles can detach the labrum from the glenoid.
Zooming into the right shoulder, viewed from the front.
The long head of biceps anchors to the superior labrum at the top of the glenoid.
In late cocking and deceleration the biceps pulls and twists this anchor.
The labrum and biceps anchor peel off the superior glenoid: a type II SLAP lesion.
In throwers the detachment can extend backward along the posterosuperior labrum.
Chronic superior instability may be followed by partial cuff tears from inside the joint.
Many shoulders have labral tears without pain, so imaging must fit the history and examination.
Schematic of the biceps anchor: aligned collagen (the labrum itself is fibrocartilage).
Repeated cocking and pulling straighten the crimped fibres at the anchor.
Torsion and traction push the fibres beyond their elastic range.
The fibres fail where the anchor meets the glenoid rim.
Small vessels bleed locally.
Inflammation clears debris, diluted by synovial fluid.
Fibroblasts lay down disorganised collagen, but no bridging scar forms across the gap.
The attachment may stay lax, so strength and control carry the load.
